sources.title: Addressing Cognitive Fog in Long-COVID-19 Patients
sources.key_finding: Terminated after n=7; no efficacy evaluable; reason: evolving nature of COVID cognitive fog / infeasible to collect enough data.

sources.title: Successful Treatment of Post-COVID-19 ADHD-like Syndrome: A Case Report
sources.key_finding: Methylphenidate/lisdexamfetamine case improvement only; not Adderall RCT evidence.

synthesis: The only registered Adderall/amphetamine-dextroamphetamine trial for Long COVID cognitive fog (NCT05597722, Phase 4) was terminated at n=7 with no analyzable efficacy endpoints. Literature is limited to stimulant prescribing association studies and non-Adderall case reports. No peer-reviewed RCT supports efficacy for established Long COVID. Tier C remains appropriate as an early/candidate signal only—not clinical efficacy.
limitations: Sole interventional registry study terminated (n=7) without efficacy results (NCT05597722). No peer-reviewed RCT of amphetamine-dextroamphetamine for Long COVID. Case-level stimulant reports are not generalizable. Stimulant harms (CV, dependence, appetite) not characterized in this population.
confidence_notes: Prior reviewers MattH55+evidence-eval-bot (2026-09-19) graded C/published; deep-dive retains C. Off-target Europe-PMC PMIDs from prior eval removed.

sources.title: A Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled, Randomized, Clinical Trial of the TLR-3 Agonist Rintatolimod in Severe Cases of Chronic Fatigue Syndrome
sources.key_finding: Sponsor ITT: placebo-adjusted exercise-tolerance improvement 21.3% (p=0.047); FDA reanalysis p=0.10 for primary.

sources.title: The Study of the Safety and Efficacy of Ampligen in Chronic Fatigue Syndrome
sources.key_finding: n=234 completed; results not posted on CT.gov (published separately as PMID 22431963).

sources.title: FDA Complete Response Letter declining Ampligen NDA for CFS
sources.key_finding: FDA CRL Feb 2013: insufficient substantial evidence of efficacy; requested additional controlled trial.

synthesis: Historical Phase 3 (AMP-516, n=234) published in PLoS One (Strayer 2012) reported modest exercise-tolerance benefit on sponsor analysis, but FDA disagreed on statistical significance of the pivotal primary and issued a Complete Response Letter (2013) declining approval, citing efficacy and safety-database deficiencies. Not FDA-approved for ME/CFS in the US; remains experimental/orphan-context candidate. Tier C (early/contested clinical signal) is correct—not B.
limitations: FDA and sponsor disagree on AMP-516 primary p-value (0.10 vs 0.047). No US approval; CRL required another controlled trial. Safety signals cited by FDA (thrombosis, cardiac events, infusion reactions/unblinding risk). Limited independent replication. Results not posted on CT.gov for NCT00215800.
confidence_notes: Prior MattH55+evidence-eval-bot C/published retained. Replaced off-target TLR review PMIDs with primary AMP-516 + regulatory record.

sources.title: Comparison of adaptive pacing therapy, cognitive behaviour therapy, graded exercise therapy, and specialist medical care for chronic fatigue syndrome (PACE): a randomised trial
sources.key_finding: Reported CBT/GET benefit on primary outcomes; subsequent reanalyses, outcome-definition changes, and patient-community critique make disease-modifying interpretation contested.

sources.title: NICE NG206 Myalgic encephalomyelitis (or encephalopathy)/chronic fatigue syndrome: diagnosis and management
sources.key_finding: Does not recommend CBT as a curative/disease-modifying treatment for ME/CFS; CBT may be offered only as supportive care for distress/symptoms if patient wants it.

sources.title: CDC ME/CFS clinical care
sources.key_finding: Emphasizes pacing and avoiding forced graded exercise; CBT not framed as cure.

synthesis: CBT for ME/CFS remains highly contested. PACE (White et al., Lancet 2011) reported benefit but is widely disputed (outcome thresholds, harms/PEM, reanalyses). NICE NG206 (2021) explicitly does not recommend CBT as curative. Framing CBT as disease-modifying treatment is not supported by current UK guideline consensus. Tier D (contested/insufficient for treats_candidate_for as efficacy claim) remains correct.
limitations: Guideline conflict (older CBT/GET-positive reviews vs NICE NG206). PACE methodological controversies. Risk of harm if CBT is paired with graded exercise that triggers PEM. Prior eval linked off-target mindfulness/meta-analysis PMIDs—replaced with PACE + NG206.
confidence_notes: Prior evidence-eval-bot D/published retained after deep-dive. Contested framing preserved.

sources.title: The Effect of Fluvoxamine and Metformin for Fatigue in Patients With Long COVID: An Adaptive Randomized Trial (REVIVE)
sources.key_finding: Fluvoxamine 100 mg BID × 60 days reduced Fatigue Severity Scale vs placebo at day 60 (−0.43) and day 90 (−0.58); metformin arm no significant fatigue benefit.

sources.title: REVIVE Trial — Long COVID
sources.key_finding: n=399 actual; primary FSS; completed; peer-reviewed as PMID 41911553.

sources.title: Fluvoxamine for Long COVID-19
sources.key_finding: n=191; CT.gov posted primary mean symptom-score change −47.3 (fluvoxamine, n=66) vs −31.1 (placebo, n=71); no statistical analysis posted; not yet clearly peer-reviewed as of deep-dive.

sources.title: COVID-OUT: metformin/ivermectin/fluvoxamine and incident long COVID
sources.key_finding: Acute fluvoxamine did NOT reduce incident long COVID (HR 1.36, 0.78–2.34)—prevention context, not treatment of established LC.

synthesis: For established Long COVID, REVIVE (Annals 2026, n≈399) reports a peer-reviewed fluvoxamine benefit on fatigue severity; a smaller CT.gov-posted RCT (NCT05874037) shows a larger numerical symptom-score drop vs placebo without posted stats/peer review. COVID-OUT shows acute fluvoxamine does not prevent incident LC. Signal is early positive for treatment of fatigue/symptoms but not guideline-consensus—tier C, not B.
limitations: REVIVE effect sizes modest; single adaptive trial. NCT05874037 lacks posted inferential stats and peer-reviewed primary paper. Acute-COVID fluvoxamine literature is a different question. Serious AEs 5/66 vs 2/71 on CT.gov posting for NCT05874037 warrant caution. Not disease-modifying consensus.
confidence_notes: Prior evidence-eval-bot C retained. Added REVIVE peer-reviewed primary; clarified prevention vs treatment.

sources.title: RECOVER-AUTONOMIC Appendix A (IVIG)
sources.key_finding: n=200 actual; primary OHQ/OIQ change over 9 months; COMPLETED but efficacy results module not posted as of 2026-09-19.

sources.title: RECOVER-AUTONOMIC Platform Protocol
sources.key_finding: Platform enrollment results only (IVIG appendix n=200); not an efficacy readout.

synthesis: NIH RECOVER-AUTONOMIC IVIG appendix (n=200) has completed enrollment/follow-up but has not posted primary efficacy results. Prior literature is case series/mechanistic. No peer-reviewed positive Phase 2/3 efficacy synthesis for IVIG in Long COVID yet. Tier C (early clinical candidate) unchanged—do not invent positive efficacy.
limitations: Efficacy results for NCT06305793 not public. Off-target PMIDs from prior eval (generic Long COVID reviews, cardiology stats) removed. Cost/access and infusion risks relevant if used off-label. Distinct from IVIG-for-POTS evidence.
confidence_notes: Prior evidence-eval-bot C retained. Waiting on RECOVER appendix A primary publication.

tier_change_why: iSTAND Phase 2 RCT (PMID 38311655) found identical 46% response with IVIG vs albumin control; no COMPASS-31 difference. Negative controlled trial → contested/insufficient (D), not early-positive C.

sources.title: Randomized controlled trial of intravenous immunoglobulin for autoimmune postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (iSTAND)
sources.key_finding: n=30; IVIG vs albumin 12 weeks; symptom response 46% both arms; COMPASS-31 change NS (p=0.629).

sources.title: The evidence for treatments for postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome: a systematic review of randomized trials
sources.key_finding: Summarizes limited RCT evidence for POTS pharmacologic options including IVIG.

sources.title: RECOVER-AUTONOMIC IVIG (Long COVID autonomic/OI)
sources.key_finding: Long COVID orthostatic intolerance population—not classic POTS primary; results pending.

synthesis: Best available controlled evidence (iSTAND 2024) does not show IVIG superiority over albumin volume-expansion control in presumed autoimmune POTS. Open-label enthusiasm and case series remain, and commentators argue dose/duration/control limitations, but for graph grading a negative small RCT without confirmatory positive RCTs warrants tier D (insufficient/contested), not C.
limitations: iSTAND small (n=30), short (12 weeks), low-dose IVIG; albumin control may mask volume effects. Patient-selection (autoimmune POTS) limits generalizability. RECOVER IVIG is Long COVID OI, not idiopathic POTS. Prior off-target PMIDs removed.
confidence_notes: Prior evidence-eval-bot C upgraded→D after iSTAND primary. Keep published; not medical advice.

sources.title: NICE NG95 Lyme disease
sources.key_finding: Recommends antibiotics (doxycycline/amoxicillin/cefuroxime); ivermectin not a recommended Lyme therapy.

sources.title: IDSA/AAN/ACR 2020 Lyme guidelines
sources.key_finding: Standard antibiotic regimens; no role for ivermectin.

sources.title: Randomized Trial of Metformin, Ivermectin, and Fluvoxamine for Covid-19 (COVID-OUT)
sources.key_finding: Ivermectin arm is for acute COVID—not Lyme; listed only to flag prior eval's incorrect NCT04510194 linkage.

synthesis: No credible clinical trials support ivermectin for Lyme disease or PTLDS. Major guidelines (NICE NG95, IDSA/AAN/ACR 2020) recommend antibiotics and do not include ivermectin. Prior eval incorrectly linked COVID-OUT. Tier D correct.
limitations: Absence of evidence is not a systematic 'empty review' formalized here, but guideline omission plus lack of PubMed interventional trials is decisive for D. Do not cite acute-COVID ivermectin trials as Lyme evidence.
confidence_notes: Prior evidence-eval-bot D retained. Removed COVID-OUT as a Lyme source.

sources.title: COVID-OUT long COVID incidence secondary outcome
sources.key_finding: Ivermectin during acute COVID: HR 0.99 (0.59–1.64) for incident long COVID—no prevention benefit.

sources.title: COVID-OUT acute severity primary
sources.key_finding: Ivermectin did not prevent severe COVID progression vs placebo.

sources.title: COVID-OUT
sources.key_finding: Acute outpatient treatment; not a trial of ivermectin for established Long COVID.

synthesis: No adequate RCT tests ivermectin as treatment for established Long COVID. Best related randomized evidence (COVID-OUT) shows no reduction in incident long COVID when given acutely, and no acute severity benefit. Tier D (insufficient/contested) correct—do not invent positive efficacy.
limitations: Prevention ≠ treatment of established PASC. Observational/anecdotal ivermectin-for-LC claims are uncontrolled. Regulatory/public-health bodies have warned against ivermectin for COVID outside trials.
confidence_notes: Prior evidence-eval-bot D retained after primary-source check.

sources.title: Use of lisdexamfetamine dimesylate in treatment of executive functioning deficits and chronic fatigue syndrome: a double blind, placebo-controlled study
sources.key_finding: n=26 adults with CFS + executive deficits; LDX improved BRIEF-A (d≈1.46) and reduced fatigue/pain vs placebo over 6 weeks.

sources.title: Efficacy and Safety of Lisdexamfetamine Dimesylate in Adults With Chronic Fatigue Syndrome
sources.key_finding: Registry record corresponding to Young 2013 cohort (small single-center).

synthesis: One small single-center RCT (Young 2013, n=26) shows short-term executive-function and fatigue improvements with LDX in CFS patients selected for executive deficits. No large confirmatory Phase 3. Stimulant risks apply. Tier C appropriate.
limitations: Very small n; 6-week duration; CFS criteria era may not match modern ME/CFS (CCC/IOM) with PEM emphasis; primary endpoint was BRIEF-A not PEM/function. Industry-relevant stimulant class harms. No replication Phase 3.
confidence_notes: Prior evidence-eval-bot C retained. Replaced off-target PMIDs with Young 2013 primary.

sources.title: COVID-OUT: outpatient metformin and incidence of post-COVID-19 condition
sources.key_finding: Acute metformin reduced provider-diagnosed long COVID by day 300: 6.3% vs 10.4%, HR 0.59 (0.39–0.89). This is PREVENTION of incident LC, not treatment of established LC.

sources.title: COVID-OUT acute primary outcomes
sources.key_finding: Metformin reduced acute severe COVID composite vs placebo.

sources.title: REVIVE: fluvoxamine and metformin for Long COVID fatigue
sources.key_finding: Metformin 750 mg BID for established Long COVID fatigue: no significant FSS benefit vs placebo.

sources.title: Metformin for fatigue in adolescent Long COVID
sources.key_finding: Estimated n=16; status UNKNOWN; not a confirmatory treatment trial.

synthesis: Strong randomized signal that early outpatient metformin reduces incidence of long COVID after acute infection (COVID-OUT). That is prevention, not treatment. For established Long COVID fatigue, REVIVE (2026) found no significant metformin benefit. Therefore the treats_candidate_for claim for established Long COVID stays C (not B): interesting related pharmacology, but treatment evidence is negative/limited.
limitations: CRITICAL: do not conflate COVID-OUT prevention HR 0.59 with efficacy in established PASC. REVIVE metformin arm negative for fatigue. Adolescent NCT06147050 too small/unknown status. Overweight/obesity COVID-OUT population limits generalizability of prevention finding.
confidence_notes: Prior evidence-eval-bot C retained with sharpened prevention≠treatment synthesis and REVIVE negative treatment arm.

tier_change_why: Two independent Phase 2 RCTs of nirmatrelvir/ritonavir for established PASC are negative: STOP-PASC (PMID 38848477) and RECOVER-VITAL (PMID 42673984, Lancet Infect Dis 2026). Observational signals for acute Paxlovid reducing later LC risk do not establish treatment efficacy. Contested/insufficient → D.

sources.title: STOP-PASC: Nirmatrelvir-Ritonavir and Symptoms in Adults With PASC
sources.key_finding: n=155; 15-day NMV/r vs placebo-ritonavir; no significant improvement in pooled 6-symptom severity at 10 weeks; stopped early for futility.

sources.title: RECOVER-VITAL: nirmatrelvir–ritonavir targeting viral persistence in long COVID
sources.key_finding: n≈959; 15- or 25-day Paxlovid vs control; no improvement in cognitive, autonomic, or exercise-intolerance clusters vs placebo.

sources.title: Paxlovid for Treatment of Long Covid (STOP-PASC)
sources.key_finding: CT.gov results align with published null primary.

sources.title: RECOVER-VITAL Appendix (Paxlovid)
sources.key_finding: Posted cluster improvement percentages similar across 25-day, 15-day, and control arms.

synthesis: Mixed observational literature suggested acute Paxlovid might reduce later Long COVID risk, but randomized treatment of established PASC is consistently negative across STOP-PASC and the large NIH RECOVER-VITAL trial (2026). Candidate treatment claim is therefore contested/insufficient (D), not early-positive C. Acute COVID indication remains separate.
limitations: Observational prevention-of-LC associations ≠ treatment of established PASC. STOP-PASC used 15-day course; RECOVER-VITAL tested 15 and 25 days—both null. Viral-persistence hypothesis not supported by these clinical endpoints. Drug-drug interactions via ritonavir remain relevant.
confidence_notes: Prior evidence-eval-bot C → D after STOP-PASC + RECOVER-VITAL primary review.

sources.title: B-Lymphocyte Depletion in Patients With ME/CFS: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Trial (RituxME)
sources.key_finding: n=151; response 26.0% rituximab vs 35.1% placebo (P=0.22); no fatigue-score difference over 24 months; more SAEs with rituximab.

sources.title: Benefit from B-lymphocyte depletion using rituximab in CFS: Phase 2
sources.key_finding: Earlier small positive signal not confirmed by Phase 3.

sources.title: Clinical impact of B-cell depletion with rituximab in CFS: case series
sources.key_finding: Hypothesis-generating only.

sources.title: RituxME Phase 3
sources.key_finding: Completed; results published as PMID 30934066 (not posted as CT.gov results module).

synthesis: RituxME Phase 3 definitively failed to confirm earlier Phase 2 optimism. Rituximab is not an effective ME/CFS therapy on current evidence. Tier D correct.
limitations: Self-reported primary outcomes; Canadian consensus population 2–15 years duration. Serious adverse events more frequent with rituximab (26% vs 19%). Do not extrapolate oncology B-cell depletion anecdotes.
confidence_notes: Prior evidence-eval-bot D retained; cited negative Phase 3 primary.

sources.title: Growth hormone treatment for neurologic symptoms of post-acute sequelae of COVID-19
sources.key_finding: n=13 PASC with low stimulated GH; 9 months rhGH improved fatigue/mood/QoL subjectively; cognition/physical performance not clearly improved; symptoms returned after stopping.

sources.title: Brain and Gut Plasticity in Mild TBI or Post-acute COVID Syndrome Following Growth Hormone Therapy
sources.key_finding: n=72 total including mTBI and PASC arms; CT.gov body-composition endpoints; not a blinded PASC symptom-efficacy RCT.

synthesis: Only a tiny open-label pilot supports symptomatic GH replacement in a selected neurologic-PASC subgroup with low stimulated GH. CT.gov body-composition data do not establish clinical efficacy. Tier C (early/mechanistic-clinical) correct—not B.
limitations: n=13 open-label; selection requires documented low GH response; symptoms rebound on cessation; no placebo control for symptom outcomes; GH costs/risks (edema, glucose, IGF-1 monitoring). NCT03554265 mixes mTBI and PASC.
confidence_notes: Prior evidence-eval-bot C retained; replaced off-target PMIDs with Wright 2024 primary.
